'''Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda''' (c. 1941 – February 1, 2014) was a [[Cameroon]]ian [[novelist]], [[chemist]], and [[paramount chief]] of the {{ill|Ewondo people|fr|Ewondo (peuple)|lt=Ewondo}} and {{ill|Bane people|fr|Bané (peuple)|lt=Bene}} people.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":10" /> Early in life, Ahanda worked for the Chemistry Department of the [[University of Yaoundé]]. She later moved to the [[Republic of the Congo]] with her husband, [[Jean Baptiste Assiga Ahanda]], and took to writing. When they returned to Cameroon, Ahanda became an elected delegate in the [[National Assembly of Cameroon]], a position she held from 1983 to 1988. Ahanda became the Ewondo paramount chief in 1999.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Romancières africaines d'expression française : le sud du Sahara|author=Noakes, Beverley Ormerod|date=1994|publisher=L'Harmattan|others=Volet, Jean-Marie, 1947–|isbn=2738422055|location=Paris|oclc=30468149}}</ref> In December 2000, she began renovating her father's palace at [[Efoulan]], [[Yaoundé]], a project that cost an estimated 150,000,000 [[CFA franc|francs&nbsp;CFA]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://www.cameroon-info.net/article/le-chateau-charles-atangana-sera-enfin-sauve-56148.html|title=Le château Charles Atangana sera enfin sauvé|website=www.cameroon-info.net|language=fr|access-date=2018-06-10|archive-date=2018-06-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612173501/http://www.cameroon-info.net/article/le-chateau-charles-atangana-sera-enfin-sauve-56148.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Ahanda is the daughter of [[Charles Atangana]]—paramount chief of the Ewondo and Bene peoples under the [[German Empire|German]] and [[French Third Republic|French]] [[colonialism|colonial]] regimes—by his second wife, Julienne Ngonoa.<ref name=":7" />

== Early life and education ==
Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda (born Marie-Thérèse Atangana) was raised as a [[princess]] alongside her brother, [[prince]] [[René Grégoire Atangana]], in [[Yaoundé|Yaoundé, Cameroon]]. She also had one half sister, [[Catherine Edzimbi Atangana]], and one half brother, [[Jean Ndengue Atangana]]. Both of her half-siblings were from her father's first marriage to [[Marie Biloa]], and they were born around forty years before she was.<ref name=":7">{{Cite news|url=http://www.bonaberi.com/article.php?aid=7|title=Bonaberi.com : A la découverte de Charles Atangana|work=Bonaberi.com|access-date=2018-05-14|language=fr|archive-date=2017-10-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171023041103/http://www.bonaberi.com/article.php?aid=7|url-status=live}}</ref> She was the daughter of [[Julienne (Yuliana) Ngonoa]] and [[Charles Atangana|Charles Antangana]], the paramount chief of the Ewondo and Bene people.<ref name=":7" />

Ahanda's father, Charles Atangana, also known as Ntsama Atangana (birth name) or Karl Atangana (German name), died only two years after her birth in 1943.<ref name=":7" /> Charles Atangana always kept friendly ties to both the German and French colonial administrations. His companionship with many of the German and French officials was said to have aided in his political advancement. He was also an advocate for the [[westernization]] of Yaoundé and Cameroonian culture.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dacb.org/stories/cameroon/ntsama-charles/|title=Ntsama, Charles Atangana|website=dacb.org|language=en|access-date=2018-05-14|archive-date=2018-06-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612142119/https://dacb.org/stories/cameroon/ntsama-charles/|url-status=live}}</ref> His rule has been both criticized and commended globally. Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda explains her father's legacy in a short biography she wrote on him,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bonaberi.com : A la découverte de Charles Atangana |url=https://www.bonaberi.com/article.php?aid=7 |access-date=2024-02-10 |website=Bonaberi.com |language=fr |archive-date=2023-02-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230226155731/https://www.bonaberi.com/article.php?aid=7 |url-status=live }}</ref> but also touches on themes of colonization in Cameroon in some of the other written works, (see [[Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda#Works and Publications|Works and Publications]] below).<ref name=":7" />

Most of Ahanda's schooling took place in Europe before the 1950s.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|url=http://www.cameroon-info.net/article/cameroun-necrologie-la-reine-des-ewondo-est-decedee-217725.html|title=Nécrologie: La reine des Ewondo est décédée|website=www.cameroon-info.net|language=fr|access-date=2018-05-14|archive-date=2018-05-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180504064017/http://www.cameroon-info.net/article/cameroun-necrologie-la-reine-des-ewondo-est-decedee-217725.html|url-status=live}}</ref> As a princess, she had access to formal education which gave her opportunities to explore different disciplines. It was through her father's loyalty to the colonial administrations, and the power he received through it, that she was able to grow up with these opportunities. The Western-style education she received was highly influential to her writing as well.<ref name=":12" />

== Personal life ==
In the early 1970s, she married Jean Baptiste Assiga Ahanda, a finance manager from Yaoundé who later held a prominent position at [[Bank of Central African States|Banque des États de l'Afrique Centrale]] (BEAC; English: The Bank of Central African States).<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cameroon-info.net/article/beac-sadou-hayatou-nest-plus-le-directeur-national-108576.html|title=Béac : Sadou Hayatou n'est plus le directeur national|website=www.cameroon-info.net|language=fr|access-date=2018-06-11|archive-date=2018-06-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612190907/http://www.cameroon-info.net/article/beac-sadou-hayatou-nest-plus-le-directeur-national-108576.html|url-status=live}}</ref> She then moved to Congo with him for several years before returning to Cameroon where they lived until she died in 2014.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|url=http://aflit.arts.uwa.edu.au/AssigaAhandaMarieTherese.html|title=Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda|website=aflit.arts.uwa.edu.au|access-date=2018-05-14}}</ref> She was married to Jean Baptiste for roughly 40 years, and together they had four children and multiple grandchildren.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":10">{{Cite news|url=https://www.journalducameroun.com/la-reine-marie-therese-assiga-ahanda-est-decedee/|title=La reine Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda est décédée |date=2014-02-03|work=Journal du Cameroun|access-date=2018-05-14|language=fr-FR|archive-date=2021-06-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210606185713/https://www.journalducameroun.com/la-reine-marie-therese-assiga-ahanda-est-decedee/|url-status=live}}</ref> Although they were together for a long time, their marriage was controversial to many.<ref name=":8" /> Jean Baptiste was of the large Etoudi clan, which was outside of her own clan. Most of this controversy surrounding their marriage was based on questions as to why they were married and if there were any political incentive or gain.<ref name=":8" />

== Professional life ==
Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda ventured into many disciplines after receiving her education in Europe and returning to Yaoundé. She first worked as a chemist in her early life before getting involved in politics. She worked for a few years at the [[University of Yaoundé]] in the science department for her career in [[chemistry]].<ref name=":9" />

=== Author ===
After doing chemistry for a few years, Ahanda took to writing books and articles. Her main goal as an [[author]] was to make her mark in history.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=D'Almeida|first=Irène Assiba|author-link=Irène Assiba d'Almeida|date=Summer 1995|title=Review of: Romancières africaines d'expression française: le sud du Sahara by Beverley Ormerod and Jean-Marie Volet|journal=Research in African Literatures|volume=26|pages=199–202|jstor=}}</ref> Some of her published works include:

* ''[[Sociétés africaines et 'High Society': Petite ethnologie de l'arrivisme]]'' (1978)
* ''Je suis raciste'' (1982)
* "Turbulences" in ''Mots Pluriels'' (1999)

These works were published after Cameroon's independence in 1960.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Historical Dictionary of the Republic of Cameroon|last=DeLancey|first=Mark|publisher=Scarecrow Press|year=2010|isbn=978-0-8108-7399-5|location=Lanham, Maryland|pages=xxxii}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Voicing the Voiceless: Contributions to Closing Gaps in Cameroon|last=Nkwi|first=Walter Gam|publisher=Langaa Research & Publishing Common Initiative Group|year=2010|isbn=978-9956-616-40-4|location=Bamenda, Cameroon|pages=172}}</ref> The novel ''Sociétés africaines et 'High Society': Petite ethnologie de l'arrivisme'' touches on themes of westernization and colonialism. It is about a young couple, Mathilde and Vincent, who both lived abroad and received Western education. When they came back to their homeland, they were astonished by the after effects of colonial rule, such as post-colonial [[corruption]]. They later became obsessed with power and found themselves intertwined in the system.<ref name=":9" /> Ahanda also uses Mathilde to draw upon the theme of [[sexism]] in the novel. Mathilde, the main female character's intelligence is highly underestimated and disregarded by most of the authoritative characters.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal|last=Brière|first=Eloise A.|date=March 2016|title=Writing in Cameroon, the first hundred years|journal=Tydskrif vir Letterkunde|volume=53|pages=51–65| issue=1 |doi=10.4314/tvl.v53i1.4|doi-access=free}}</ref> This was said to highlight societal or [[Oppression|systematic oppression]] that most women face, in order to motivate her female readers to improve their situations.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Dehon|first=Claire L.|date=Spring 1996|title=Women in Black African Novels Written in French|journal=NWSA Journal|volume=8|pages=110–123|jstor=}}</ref>

This novel also indicates the importance of [[individualism]] and individual rights in combating [[Neocolonialism|neo-colonialism]].<ref name=":1" /> However, this individualistic perspective may come from the influence of the Westernized notion of individualism, as opposed to [[Collectivism and individualism|collectivism]] seen in the [[tradition]]al village system. In other words, through her writing she uses colonial influences to fight neo-colonialism.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Critical Perspectives on Mongo Beti|last=Arnold|first=Stephen H.|publisher=Lynne Rienner Publishers|year=1998|isbn=0-89410-586-8|location=Boulder, Colorado|pages=305–314}}</ref>

=== Deputy of the National Assembly ===
After publishing her first two novels, Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda returned to Cameroon. She served as a [[Deputy (legislator)|deputy]] for the [[National Assembly (Cameroon)|National Assembly of Cameroon]] for five years, between 1983 and 1988.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /><ref name=":11">{{Cite news|url=http://evopra.over-blog.com/article-16640138.html|title=Marie-Thérèse Assiga Atangana |last=Eva|work=Le blog de Eva Hendrickx|access-date=2018-05-14|language=fr-FR|archive-date=2018-06-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612140847/http://evopra.over-blog.com/article-16640138.html|url-status=live}}</ref> As a previous chemist and author, this was her first experience of political involvement outside of the duties of being a princess. She did however understand politics, corruption, and history through the research she conducted for her novel ''Sociétés africaines et 'High Society': Petite ethnologie de l'arrivisme''.<ref name=":0" /> Cameroonian president [[Ahmadou Ahidjo]] resigned in 1982, and [[Paul Biya]], the prime minister at the time, took over. Ahanda was mostly instrumental in making decisions regarding [[chiefdom]]s, or the hierarchical system of chiefs.<ref name=":7" />

Years prior to Ahanda's birth, before any colonial figures came to that region of Cameroon, the chief of the [[Etoa Meki]] village (present day Yaoundé) was [[Essono Ela]].<ref name=":8" /> When the German colonial administration came in, they appointed Charles Atangana as chief supreme, and imprisoned Essono Ela in front of his people. Essono Ela was considered a rebel in the eyes of the colonial administration.<ref name=":8" /> Essono Ela's nephew, [[Fouda Anaba]], became a very powerful and influential individual in politics. He had a strong relationship with president [[Ahmadou Ahidjo]], and allegedly persuaded some of his decisions. Fouda Anaba advocated for getting rid of the position of superior chief of the Ewondo and Bene people as he felt this specific position was reignited by the German colonial administration. His advocating worked, and this position, along with many other traditional systems were uprooted.<ref name=":8" />

In 1977 after independence, the constitutional decree #77/609 called for the restoration of these traditional systems alongside the current political system.<ref name=":13">{{Cite book|title=Diagnostic de la délinquance urbaine à Yaoundé|date=2002|publisher=[UN-HABITAT]|others=United Nations Human Settlements Programme., UNDP., Cameroon.|isbn=9212310478|location=Nairobi|oclc=84305318}}</ref> During her time as a deputy, Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda fought for the reestablishment of this position and adherence to constitutional decree #77/609.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":8" /> If this were to be achieved, she would be throned as chief of the Ewondo and Bene people, as it was her traditional blood right.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://nanjecreativethinking.blogspot.com/2012/08/chieftaincy-law-organizing-chiefdoms-in.html|title=Chieftaincy Law: Organizing Chiefdoms in Cameroon|website=nanjecreativethinking.blogspot.com|access-date=2018-06-10|date=2012-08-29|archive-date=2018-06-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612141045/https://nanjecreativethinking.blogspot.com/2012/08/chieftaincy-law-organizing-chiefdoms-in.html|url-status=live}}</ref> She was confronted with much backlash from many Ewondo people, not because of the colonial ties to her father, but mainly because she was a woman.<ref name=":8" /> It was not customary among the Ewondo for women to hold such high positions of power. Her own marriage also caused controversy since she married outside of her clan. Because of these two aspects, many Ewondo people, including some members of her own family denounced her title.<ref name=":8" />

=== Chieftaincy ===
After the decree #77/609 was successfully implemented in the 1990s, most [[ethnic groups in Cameroon]] had reestablished chieftaincies. There were three levels of chieftaincies that were described in the constitutional decree.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":2" /> The third degree chieftaincies are representatives of their distinct territories in each neighborhood. Second degree chieftaincies are representatives of groups of neighborhoods in a certain area. The first degree chieftaincies are representatives of entire districts (known as [[paramount chief]]s).<ref name=":2" /> In Yaoundé there are around 350 third degree chiefs, 7 second degree chiefs, and one first degree chief.<ref name=":13" />

In 1999 Marie-Thérèse Assiga Ahanda was the first female to be throned paramount chief of the Ewondo and Bene people- the official title of Yaoundé's first degree chief. She served as the chief of the Ewondo and Bene people of Yaoundé for fifteen years (1999–2014).<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":12" /><ref name=":11" /> Her coronation ceremony took place in Yaoundé and lasted several hours.<ref name=":3" /> It was filled with performances, decor, and practices from both Cameroonian and European influences. Hundreds of guests were invited to the event, and many tuned in to local TV and radio broadcasting to experience it live.<ref name=":3">{{Citation|last=Thomas D'Aquin|title=Marie Thérèse Atangana : Une Reine à Yaoundé |date=2014-02-03|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sjm319PGjgc |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211213/sjm319PGjgc |archive-date=2021-12-13 |url-status=live|access-date=2018-05-23}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

There was much controversy concerning her appointment to this position, mostly due to traditional, gendered, and political concerns. Many people felt that she would not be qualified for the position because of her marriage as well as her status as a woman.<ref name=":8" /> She fought for her right to be on the throne, while in the process losing much support from not only public figures, but family as well.<ref name=":8" />

There is currently no successor for the title of paramount chief of the Ewondo and Bene people.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":8" />

== Death ==
Ahanda died on February 1, 2014, at the age of seventy-two.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":8" /> Her health was said to have been declining in her final years. She made very little public appearances, and dedicated most of her resources towards the rehabilitation of her father's palace in Yaoundé as a landmark.<ref name=":4" /> Her death was said to be peaceful, however the public was not given much detail about it or the happenings in the royal home at the time. It was noted that she was a fairly private individual herself.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":8" />
